A smartwatch's longevity depends on two primary factors: the hardware that makes up the device and the software that allows it to be put to use. A watch can feel outdated if its software support has ended, despite the touchscreens, sensors, and batteries working just fine. Tech companies notoriously limit software support for different devices, in part to encourage the purchase of newer models, and in part because older hardware can struggle with newer software features. No matter how stylish an Apple Watch remains over time, any smartwatch's usefulness will depend on the manufacturer's commitment to software updates. On the hardware side, users can get more life out of their smartwatch by following proper charging habits, and many manufacturers advise keeping the device away from extreme temperatures. On the software side, keeping a smartwatch's companion app updated can ensure continued compatibility with mobile devices, but larger OS updates are what will keep the watch relevant for longer. Smartwatch manufacturers all offer different longevity guarantees, so here we're taking a look at which smartwatches come with the longest software support. Samsung is known for offering long-term support across its mobile device lineups. On the phone side, Samsung currently promises up to seven years of OS and security updates for flagship Galaxy S devices. Samsung has a slightly different policy for its wearables, though for years a similar commitment has trickled down to the Galaxy Watch lineup. Historically, Samsung Galaxy Watches have received support for four years of major OS upgrades and five years of security updates. While that policy was enough for wearables like the Galaxy Watch 8 to sit above other smartwatches in terms of software support longevity, Samsung recently announced even more support. With the release of the Galaxy Watch 9 and the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2, Samsung opted to provide five major OS upgrades and five years of security patches. Samsung has improved its firmware support policies several times over the last few years as well. Some popular Galaxy Watches will lose support after 2027, including the Galaxy Watch 6, simply due to age. That said, Samsung's latest support guarantee will keep owners of the latest Galaxy Watch models updated through 2031. This puts the company's wearables line closer to its mobile devices in terms of software support longevity, and the five-year commitment is one of the best among popular smartwatch makers. Notoriously ambiguous when it comes to software support, Apple isn't as transparent about the Apple Watch lineup as Samsung is about its Galaxy Watches. The Apple Watch 12 and Ultra 4 are likely to have the longest lifespans from this point in time, but only because they're the most recent to hit the market. Models like the Apple Watch Series 11, Ultra 3, and SE 3 are still receiving support through annual watchOS updates and periodic security updates, as are even older models like the Series 9, Series 10, and Ultra 2. Apple's oldest models still receiving support are the Series 9 and Ultra 2, which were both released in 2023. But with the 2026 release of watchOS 27 came the discontinuation of support for earlier Apple Watch models, nixing the Series 6, Series 7, Series 8, SE 2, and original Apple Watch Ultra from the list of models that can still be updated. The oldest among them is the Apple Watch Series 6. It launched in 2020, which means Apple provided owners with close to six full years of software support. Not all Apple Watches received that duration of support, however, as the Series 8 and original Ultra were released in 2022, meaning they only received four years of updates. Of course, a smartwatch can continue to work beyond its officially supported software updates. Several Apple Watch owners report long lifespans out of the devices, and the discontinuation of software updates only eliminates the ability to receive the newest features and compatibility with some apps. As tech giants go, Google is one of the more transparent companies when it comes to its software support policies, even standing behind them in its marketing materials. Just like Samsung, Google provides a guaranteed seven years of OS and security updates for its Pixel phone series, which includes the recently released Google Pixel 11 lineup. But Samsung and Google differ when it comes to smartwatch support, with Google only guaranteeing three years of updates for Pixel Watches. The current generation Pixel Watch 5 launched in August of 2026 and will receive software support until October of 2029, which is good for a little more than three years. Previous generations of the Pixel Watch support Google's claim that it provides three years of software support, as the original Pixel Watch debuted in October of 2022 and Google discontinued support in October of 2025. The first Google Pixel Watch moved through two major OS upgrades during that timeframe, going from Wear OS 3.5 at launch to Wear OS 5.1. One thing to note is that Google's language often claims the company guarantees "at least" three years of software updates. While the three-year guarantee held true for the original Pixel Watch, the Pixel Watch 2 is nearing the end of its guaranteed update window. With that window set to end in October 2026, it remains to be seen if Google will extend support for the Pixel Watch 2 or start to establish a three-year pattern for its more current models. Amazfit might not carry the name recognition of some other smartwatch brands, but it's among the best cheap smartwatch brands according to users. Its latest models include the Bip 6 and Bip Max smartwatches, each of which is priced under $100. The affordability doesn't negate solid software support, with Amazfit devices typically receiving security updates every 90 days for at least two years after the smartwatch's first shipment date. Zepp Health, the company that owns Amazfit, also notes in its product support policy overview that it may support security updates for more than three years for some models. In case of extreme security vulnerabilities, even devices on their end-of-life product list may receive software support. Two years of software support doesn't necessarily provide much comfort for smartwatch purchasers, but Amazfit's commitment is still one of the best among smartwatch manufacturers. Zepp Health does a good job of keeping Amazfit smartwatch customers informed, publishing and frequently updating a list of devices and their update windows. Owners of older Amazfit smartwatches can use it to see if their device has reached its EOL declaration. Those who've purchased newer models like the Amazfit Balance, Amazfit T-Rex 3, and previously mentioned Bip 6 and Bip Max can use it to see if their devices will receive extended support over the coming years. In many ways, Garmin watches beat the Apple Watch for fitness users. However, that isn't quite the case when it comes to software support. Just like Apple, Garmin doesn't have a published software support policy or timeline for any of its smartwatches, but while Apple has established a five- to six-year pattern of software support, Garmin shows a two- to three-year pattern for its smartwatches. Its most recent flagship releases are the Fenix 9 and Fenix 9 Pro, both of which start close to the $1,000 mark. Even with such hefty price tags, Garmin doesn't guarantee feature updates through software support for these smartwatches. But its Forerunner 965 was released in March of 2023, with Garmin confirming that no new features were planned for the watch in May of 2025. Similarly, the Garmin Fenix 7 Pro hit the market in May of 2023 and was confirmed to be excluded from new features in May of 2025. Typically, Garmin smartwatches get software support until the model's newest iteration is released. But Garmin users will also acknowledge that security updates and bug fixes can continue for several years after a watch is released. In a Reddit forum, for example, the owner of a Garmin 735XT claims the smartwatch is more than eight years old and still receives occasional maintenance updates. While Garmin smartwatch owners can expect the company to restrict feature updates to encourage the purchase of newer models, it has exhibited support for security issues for years beyond the release of such models.

Perhaps this is my turbocharged Porsche 996 ownership clouding my judgement, but the car you see here might be the greatest road-going achievement in the company's long history. Just seventy examples of the 996-generation 911 GT2 Clubsport were built, and the driving experience on offer here is equal parts sublime and terrifying.  This car rides the knife edge between putting the widest smile you've ever had on your face and making you brown your trousers. If you are talented behind the wheel, it'll offer you one of the greatest driving experiences money can buy, but if you are even a little bit off your game, or you let it lull you into a false sense of security, this monster will bite back faster than you can blink. This was perhaps Porsche's last rear-wheel drive turbocharged maniac of a car, as later generations of the GT2 received more refinement and electronic enhancement. And if you act quickly, one of the seventy cars could be yours. This one is currently for sale on Bring A Trailer, with no reserve.  The market for these cars has gone bonkers, and this example being a three-time Bring-A-Trailer alum only aids in demonstrating that. In 2021, the car, then with 6,300 miles on, changed hands for a comparatively paltry $160,000. In late 2023, it was listed again with 7,000 miles on the dial and failed to sell with a high bid of $200,000. As of this writing, with several days remaining on the auction, the same car has reached a bid of $400,000, and it surely won't stop there. Motor Trend's 2002 review of the 996 GT2 warned that the car "has no inherent bad habits, but it will identify and exaggerate yours." Car and Driver held similar beliefs, describing the car as being for "serious drivers only." If that's the kind of driving experience you're looking for, and you're well-heeled enough to afford the upper-six-figure price tag this car is sure to bring, then you need to bid on it immediately. Only available in Europe as a no-cost option for any GT2 buyers, the Clubsport package brought an extra level of safety and security to the table. This package included a bolt-in roll bar with an optional front section supplied separately, GT3-style fixed-back seats covered in fire-resistant cloth, red three-point seat belts and a separate red six-point racing harness for the driver, a fire extinguisher, and a battery master shut-off switch. That may not sound like much, but it's essentially the twenty-five-year-old equivalent of Porsche's modern Weissach package, which runs tens of thousands of extra dollars on your new GT3. Even though the Clubsport package doesn't add any horsepower or mechanical tweaks of any kind, it's the kind of hardcore option that most wouldn't take. The 996 GT2 is already hardcore enough that it scarcely needs anything else to be a proper track machine. With carbon ceramic brakes, wide sticky Michelins, and as sharp a steering rack as Porsche ever installed in anything, the 996 GT2 was mind-bendingly fast for its day. There are people, myself included, who didn't believe a 911 could ever get faster than this. I still think that may be true, in terms of human speed, as modern 911s tend to do much of the driving fast on your behalf through computers.  GT2 project manager Hartmut Kristen told Car and Driver at the time, "The entire philosophy of this car is different from the Turbo's. It's for the driver who wants to be able to take his car to its absolute limits on his own." If you aren't interested in taking a car to its limits, this isn't the one for you. For a 996 GT2 Clubsport to be coddled, only taken out for your nearest cars and coffee event, it would be shameful. To fail to extract the most from this car is dereliction of ownership duties. Unlike the 911 Turbo on which this car is based, the GT2 takes things to the next level. Where the 911 Turbo was simply a Teutonic appliance built for the express purpose of speed, the GT2 was a plaything that urged the driver to be better. Ditching the Turbo's all-wheel drive, active aero, and stability management, the GT2 was more raw, more powerful (up from 414 horsepower to 456), and less weight (around 220 pounds lighter). This particular car was delivered new to Sweden and imported to the US, then federalized by a shop in California. Because it isn't demonstrably different from the U.S.-spec 996 GT2, this was allowed without much modification. Since then it has been driven just 7,714 miles, less than one mile per day of its existence. It's a shame that it's been driven so little, but in just a few days you'll probably be looking at one of the most expensive 996 sales in history. If you're the buyer and you don't immediately take this car for a twisty road trip or a track day, you're a coward in my book.

The early crop of family-friendly SUVs from the 1990s that helped popularize the body style didn't shy away from larger engines. For its debut for the 1991 model year, the Ford Explorer came with a 4.0-liter V6 powerplant. In 1993, Jeep launched the Grand Cherokee with a standard 4.0-liter or optional 5.2-liter V8. Three years later, Ford joined in by offering a 5.0-liter V8 engine in the Explorer. In short, the more cylinders, the merrier.  Fast forward to today, and over 20 three-row midsize SUVs (call some of them crossovers, if you want to get technical) from both mainstream and premium brands now offer four-cylinder mills under the hood. A few still have V6s, even fewer have V8s, like the new Dodge Durango. And the crop of full-sized SUVs still on the market have yet to downsize the engine bay. But those are the exceptions, not the rule these days. So, if a three-row SUV is on your horizon, you might want to know what's the largest one you can get with a four-cylinder engine, which translates to a bigger street presence and potentially more cabin space along with good fuel economy. Your options include everything from the Buick Enclave and Hyundai Palisade to the refined Audi Q7 and Lexus TX. We'll rank these large SUVs by total length, from longest to shortest, because that's easier to nail down and compare than passenger or cargo volume, which can be harder to judge because of sunroofs and other equipment. We'll cover the least expensive 2026 trim for each four-cylinder model, yet this isn't meant to be an exhaustive list. All MSRPs include factory destination charges, passenger/seating counts include the driver, and fuel economy ratings cover the standard four-cylinder configuration (usually with front-wheel drive). To avoid duplicating information, we'll skip platform mates of the featured SUVs, such as the Toyota Grand Highlander alongside the Lexus TX. Although the seven-seat Buick Enclave shares a platform with the Chevrolet Traverse and GMC Acadia, it's the most stretched out of the trio with a front-to-back measurement of 207.6 inches. That's just 3.7 inches short of a full-size Chevy Tahoe and the longest of any of the SUVs in this comparison. With both back rows folded, the Enclave offers 97.5 cubic feet of cargo room, putting it among the 2026 SUVs with the largest cargo capacity. Because few people complain about front-row legroom, we'll look at how much space there is to stretch out in the rear. For this Buick, that means 41.4 inches in the middle row — the most of any model on this list — and 32.1 inches in the back. The Enclave (along with the Traverse and Acadia) earns extra bragging rights: at 328 horsepower, it has more than any other non-hybrid four-cylinder competitor in its class. That output comes from a turbocharged 2.5-liter engine, which also produces 326 lb-ft of torque. The base Preferred trim with standard front-wheel drive (FWD) has an MSRP of $48,395. In this configuration, the Enclave is EPA-rated for a combined fuel economy of 22 mpg. Although the Grand Cherokee helped usher in the SUV craze, it wasn't available in three-row form until 2021. Meanwhile, 2026 marks the first year of the Grand Cherokee L with a four-cylinder powerplant. The base engine remains the 293-horsepower 3.6-liter V6 engine because Jeep treats the turbocharged 2.0-liter Hurricane 4 engine as an upgrade, so buyers have to at least step up to the Limited trim for output that increases to 324 horsepower and 332 lb-ft of torque. In this case, the price of entry begins at $48,315 for a rear-wheel-drive Limited or $48,355 for a Laredo Altitude with a 2.0-liter Hurricane 4. The engine remains the sole powerplant for all of the higher grades, up to the Summit. It gives this Jeep a fuel economy rating of 23 mpg. Sadly, the once-available 5.7-liter V8 engine was dropped in 2024 because of low demand. The stretched-out Grand Cherokee measures 204.9 inches, which translates into a maximum cargo capacity of 84.6 cubic feet. Second-row passengers will find 39.4 inches of legroom compared to 30.3 inches for the folks at the back of the bus. Depending on the trim, the Grand Cherokee L can hold six or seven people in total. Although the Lexus TX 350 and Toyota Grand Highlander share the same platform, these crossover SUVs aren't identical. The Lexus is 203.2 inches long, compared with 201.4 inches for the Toyota, which is why we've decided to focus on the TX here. The standard turbocharged 2.4-liter four-cylinder engine delivers 275 horsepower and 317 lb-ft of torque. If you're curious, the same unit in the Grand Highlander is detuned to 265 horsepower and 310 lb-ft of torque. The TX flexes its size on the inside too, with 97 cubic feet of maximum cargo space. That almost matches the Enclave, which is over 4 inches longer. Second-row legroom is 39.5 inches, which is an above-average measurement for this group, but a third row with 33.5 inches puts the TX ahead of the Buick and most others. Seating capacity ranges from six to seven, depending on the trim. With FWD, the base TX 350 edition costs $57,890 and gets 23 mpg combined. Although an all-new VW Atlas will hit the streets for 2027, the 2026 edition is still a spacious machine at 200.7 inches long. The automaker's cabin formula emphasized generous cargo space (96.6 cubic feet) and a best-of-the-list 33.7 inches of third-row legroom. The trade-off is a second row with slightly subpar 37.6 inches of legroom and near bottom-of-the-barrel standing. Still, despite being 2.5 inches shorter than the Lexus TX, the Atlas has almost as much maximum cargo space, falling short by just 0.4 cubic feet, and it always offers seven-passenger seating, regardless of trim. With a starting price of $43,135, the starter version, an SE trim with front-wheel drive, is among the least expensive options for a spacious three-row crossover. Under the hood is a familiar Volkswagen setup: a turbocharged 2.0-liter four-cylinder engine. In this application, this unit produces 269 horsepower and 273 lb-ft of torque. Fuel economy falls in line with the other SUVs on this list at a respectable 23 mpg combined. The Atlas' upscale cousin, the Audi Q7, also makes the list of larger SUVs with four-cylinder power, although the two models don't share the same platform. However, thanks to its shorter overall length (199.6 inches), the Q7 offers the least maximum cargo room (68.1 cubic feet) and the tightest third-row fit (29.2 inches of legroom). The cargo gap with the Atlas is striking for SUVs separated by just 1.1 inches in length: With both rear rows folded, the VW holds 28.5 cubic feet more. Meanwhile, 38.8 inches of second-row legroom provide more stretch-out room than the Atlas, but still trail most of the competitors covered here. Luckily, all 2026 Q7s have seven-passenger seating. With a starting price of $63,295, the 2026 Q7 is the most expensive member of the group. That's for the core Premium trim with the ubiquitous turbocharged 2.0-liter engine producing 261 horsepower and 273 lb-ft of torque. That horsepower rating is the lowest among this gang of seven SUVs, though the higher price is somewhat offset by standard all-wheel drive. Combined fuel economy for this base engine is rated at 22 mpg. The standard 2026 Hyundai Palisade doesn't make the cut because of the V6 power, but the hybrid version does. Its 2.5-liter four-cylinder engine combines turbocharging and a hybrid setup for combined output of 329 horsepower and 339 lb-ft of torque, edging out the Enclave. With the standard FWD configuration, the Palisade Hybrid starts at $45,760 for the Blue SEL trim. Thanks to hybrid technology, fuel economy is leaps and bounds above the others, with combined fuel economy at 31 to 34 mpg, depending on the trim. Most editions seat seven, but lower grades offer an eight-passenger option. Lengthwise, the Palisade Hybrid sits on the shorter side, measuring 199.2 inches front to back. However, 41.4 inches of second-row legroom places this Hyundai near the top. It's more in the middle, with 32.1 inches of third-row legroom and 86.7 cubic feet of maximum cargo space. At 198.7 inches long, the 2026 Ford Explorer is the shortest SUV covered here. This is reflected in modest second-row legroom of 37 inches — the least of any of the seven listed) and below-average third-row legroom (31.8 inches). Its 85.8 cubic feet of cargo capacity also puts the Explorer at the lower end of the range. This three-row Ford can seat six or seven people, depending on the trim. The Explorer stands out for its architecture. Like the Grand Cherokee L, it offers standard RWD, amid a sea of FWD or AWD competitors. However, unlike the Jeep, it comes standard with turbocharged four-cylinder power. In this case, it uses a 2.3-liter EcoBoost engine that makes 300 horsepower and 310 lb-ft of torque. And along with ample power, with a combined fuel economy rating of 24 mpg, the base Explorer ekes out slightly better efficiency than most of its rivals. The entry-level Active trim has an MSRP of $40,260, making the Explorer the cheapest model on the list.

Bluetooth technology has come a long way from the days of single-ear headsets. In 2026, almost everyone owns at least one pair of Bluetooth headphones or earbuds, and you can usually find multiple sales on top-tier products from companies like Sony, Bose, and Apple. But what are some of the non-negotiable features to look for in modern Bluetooth headphones? That's a fair question, and after careful consideration, we came up with four legitimate answers: active noise-canceling (ANC), strong battery life, multipoint capabilities, and a companion app. Our list runs in descending order, too, with the most important feature (ANC) leading the pack. Many of the cheapest headphones on the market are supported by some type of ANC system, so it just doesn't make sense to own a product that can't attenuate distracting noises. Sure, there are plenty of decent headphones without ANC, but we're simply not interested, and we don't think you should be either. There's plenty to discuss between all four of our Bluetooth headphones checkboxes, though, so without further ado, let's start the learning. ANC is one of the best features ever to grace a pair of headphones or earbuds; in most cases, we'd even choose an objectively bad pair of cans or buds over a product that doesn't include ANC, even if we knew the audio would be better. We won't get too in the weeds with the science, but we will provide this quick explainer: Active noise-canceling uses built-in microphones on your Bluetooth headphones and earbuds to analyze environmental sound. When distracting frequencies are detected, your headphones generate opposing sound waves to "cancel out" the unwanted noise. ANC is no longer the boutique investment it was when the technology first rolled out to consumers. It's not a feature that's merely shared by multiple manufacturers either; Brand A can wield an entirely different ANC system than Brand B. When it comes to class-leading ANC, you can always rely on companies like Bose and Sony to deliver some of the best attenuation in town. Apple is no straggler, too; the AirPods Pro 2 deliver exceptional ANC that we never, ever turn off. Audio manufacturers have also started implementing adaptive ANC systems, which automatically analyze and adjust your noise canceling in real time. This prevents you from having to open up your headphones' companion app to adjust ANC settings manually. Sennheiser even has a feature called Sound Zones, which lets you build a custom audio profile — complete with ANC and EQ settings — for a specific location. Part of what makes a pair of Bluetooth headphones or earbuds "wireless" in the first place is that they don't need to stay connected to a host device for power and audio data. In lieu of the former, headphone manufacturers build batteries into their wireless on-ear, over-ear, and in-ear products. You'd be surprised at how long some of these cells can carry a set of cans or buds; we've also been spoiled by the likes of the Sennheiser Momentum 5 (over 50 hours with ANC enabled) and the Anker Soundcore P31i (up to 7.5 hours, with four extra charges from a topped-off case). Generally speaking, we wouldn't want to own a pair of Bluetooth headphones that delivers less than 25 hours with ANC enabled; we also wouldn't suggest wireless earbuds that last less than five hours on a full charge. USB-C has all but dethroned USB-A and Micro USB when it comes to charging ports, allowing modern headphones to charge faster than ever before. But we're still betting most of us will want our daily drivers to last an entire work shift without worry, or for the majority of a cross-country flight. ANC isn't the only variable that affects battery life either; volume level and the types of audio files you listen to can have an impact, too. Customizing certain parts of the sound profile can also increase or decrease battery longevity (e.g., more bass = less battery). Debuting back in 2010, Bluetooth Multipoint was created by the Bluetooth Special Interest Group (SIG), and the feature has evolved into a staple of Bluetooth headphones and earbuds. Quite simply, Multipoint is a feature that allows you to have a single pair of headphones simultaneously paired to at least two host devices (e.g., phone, tablet, laptop). When it works correctly, Multipoint delivers an almost instantaneous switchover to a second or third device. Here's an ideal scenario: You have Multipoint enabled on your Sony WH-1000XM6, so your headphones are connected to both your smartphone and work laptop. This means you should be able to listen to tunes or watch a YouTube video on your phone, while still receiving audible notifications from your work PC. From one Bluetooth generation to the next, Multipoint has drastically improved, thanks in part to the LE Audio standard introduced with Bluetooth 5.3. While it's still not a foolproof feature, it's one we couldn't live without at this point. The writer of this article uses Sony WH-1000XM4 headphones every day with the cans paired to both a phone and a laptop. Multipoint isn't necessarily a feature you rely on all the time; it's when you know you need to divide your attention between multiple apps and devices that it comes in handy the most. Last but not least, we come to the part of the list where we discuss the ancillary software you'll be able to download for most Bluetooth headphones. Big brands like Sony, Bose, Anker, Sennheiser, and countless others offer a free companion app for wireless headphones and earbuds. Some apps are relatively basic, while others offer a dizzying array of features and customizations. There are actually two major reasons why we won't buy a pair of cans or buds that aren't supported by an app, with software updates being the first. As with our phones, tablets, computers, and game consoles, headphone developers are able to release patches to address security loopholes in their apps. Updates also allow developers to roll out new features and to improve existing capabilities. We've seen a number of headphone updates hit the market to address ANC issues across multiple brands; without access to a companion app, affected buds and cans would have no way to receive those crucial fixes. The other major reason why a companion app is a must for us is audio customization. Out of the box, most headphones deliver a warm, bass-forward sound profile that works well for music, movies, TV shows, and video games, but not everyone is going to dig the defaults. Fortunately, most headphone apps contain a library of listening presets you'll be able to choose from; many even include a graphic EQ that you can use to shape your own audio profile. Again, nothing app-related is mandatory, but it feels like a huge piece of the puzzle is missing when mobile software isn't an option.

A common rule of thumb for PC building was to allocate anywhere between 30% to 40% of the budget towards the GPU for a balanced build, but this advice doesn't really hold much ground anymore. Alongside other hardware, graphics card prices are seeing hikes quite frequently, and mid-range GPUs aren't affordable anymore. So, it goes without saying that building a budget gaming PC is more challenging than it was a couple of years back. The good part is that modern integrated graphics are changing the equation and playing a big role in keeping budget PC builds alive. Old integrated GPUs that used to ship with Intel and AMD APUs could barely handle anything beyond displaying the desktop, but that's not true of modern iGPUs. Recent Intel Arc and AMD Radeon integrated graphics are surprisingly capable. Of course, on the desktop end, there aren't many options, but the Zen 4-based AMD Ryzen 8000G series is still holding its ground in the current market. The Ryzen 7 8700G, in particular, is a decent pick for anyone who is looking to build a budget gaming PC. This APU packs the Radeon 780M, which is the same iGPU that powers popular gaming handhelds like the Asus ROG Ally X and Lenovo Legion Go. It's also not far behind the newer Radeon 890M in the current-gen Xbox Ally X and Legion Go 2. Specifically, per gaming benchmarks, the difference can be anywhere between 20% and 35% in 1080p gaming. The Ryzen 5 8600G is also a good pick, especially for those with a very tight budget. It comes with the slightly less capable Radeon 760M, comparable to the iGPU in the custom APU inside the Steam Deck. I don't feel the need to rush out and buy a graphics card for the time being. Needless to say, the Radeon 780M or the 760M can't smoothly handle everything you throw at it. Even with the visual settings turned down, the iGPUs can struggle to offer a playable experience on some titles. The good part is that technologies such as AMD FSR can make up for the lack of raw power to some degree. These technologies don't suddenly turn an iGPU into a dGPU, but they can improve perceived smoothness through frame generation and upscaling. Of course, not all games come with AMD FSR baked into them, and that's where tools like Lossless Scaling and Optiscaler step in. With the right combination of settings and frame generation technologies, the expectations around budget gaming can change. A little extra frame generation never hurt anyone.  A dedicated GPU can take up a significant portion of the budget in a new PC build, which can leave less money for the other core parts. An APU with a capable iGPU, on the other hand, lets you spread that cost over time. It wouldn't be a good idea to buy whatever graphics card fits the budget now and settle for a setup that can't deliver the desired level of performance. This also makes sense given the current GPU market, as buying GPUs at retail prices isn't the wisest move for those seeking the best bang for the buck. However, it's important to pair the APU with the right memory, as it can make or break the iGPU performance. Speed makes a difference, and sometimes you can get a boost without reaching in your wallet While integrated graphics play a big role in budget PC builds, an APU isn't always the better choice. For instance, a build that focuses on 1440p or 4K gaming can't really rely on the iGPU if it's expected to run anything beyond indie games or old-school emulation. Integrated graphics also share system memory with the CPU, whereas dGPUs have dedicated VRAM, which matters for tasks such as 3D rendering, video editing, and AI workloads. Even so, if you mainly want to play lighter games, handle lightweight workloads, and plan to add a dGPU later, starting with integrated graphics can be a sensible approach. Scoring illegal sex along Queens’ Roosevelt Avenue has never been easier — as the number of hookers has multiplied and prostitution-related arrests have plunged by 60% along the seedy strip since soft-on-crime socialist Zohran Mamdani became mayor this year. John, a 40-year-old Manhattan horndog, said he has no problem schlepping on the subway to the notorious open-air sex bazaar — nicknamed the “Market of Sweethearts” — because the women are “cheap” and cops have their hands tied by lax laws and policies. There, scantily-clad streetwalkers brazenly solicit passersby around the clock, offering “happy ending” massages and more in front of rows of two-story commercial buildings. Often the activity occurs within sight of cops on patrol. The hookers walk their wide-eyed customers inside dozens of illegally operating brothels throughout the avenue’s red-light district, which stretches roughly two miles through Jackson Heights and Corona. “I can get it done for $60 to $80,” boasted John. “In Manhattan . . .  it costs $200 to $300.” Negotiating a tryst is “super easy,” he added. “They just show up and that’s it, and when I get bored with those women, I head to Flushing. “The Chinese women charge $60 for sex and $40 for oral sex,” he said. “They’re open to sex without a condom for $100 or more. “Latinas are more expensive. With the Chinese women, you get 30 minutes; the Latinas are obsessed with watching the clock.” He said the woman lead customers to a “place upstairs, in very small rooms.” A Post reporter last week visited Roosevelt Avenue near 90th Street and spotted nine Asian women turning tricks while two others acted as hostesses or managers. They all declined to comment. However, when the reporter later approached a group of Ecuadorian sex workers, they began competing for his business. One offered “massages” using “three positions” running $100 for 20 minutes — which included $50 to rent time in a room of a nearby building. The second woman offered a discount: “I can [give] you the hour for $300. Normally it’s just 15 minutes, but a half hour we can do it for $150. I give you four positions. We can do whatever.” Clusters of New York City have been inundated with hookers and pimps brazenly operating on public streets since a state statute prohibiting loitering for the purpose of prostitution was repealed by far-left Albany pols in February 2021. The change in the law has allowed hookers to operate more freely, with cops turning their attention to traffickers, pimps and johns. NYPD officers reported making 193 prostitution-related arrests along Roosevelt Avenue this year through Sept. 13, records show. That’s a massive 59% drop from the 468 arrests during the same period the previous year when ex-NYPD captain-turned-mayor Eric Adams and NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch led a major enforcement effort dubbed “Operation Restore Roosevelt.” The raids put a major dent in the migrant sex-peddling strip. Major crimes like murders and shootings along the same corridor are down 3%. Former state Sen. Hiram Monserrate said there’s no doubt that illegal prostitution and sex-trafficking markets have flourished along Roosevelt Avenue since Mamdani became mayor, largely because Hizzoner is making it more difficult for cops to enforce the law. “It is becoming apparent that there is less enforcement, and I think that comes from the top.” said Monserrate, now a local Democratic district leader representing the besieged neighborhoods. “The current formula is not working to keep our community safe. It’s a disaster. The problem has gotten worse, and this administration has done nothing to correct it.” “Restore, rinse, release — that’s the problem with Roosevelt Avenue,” said a city government official. “The cops catch these johns and put them away, but they pop up like whack-a-mole. Enough is enough. Someone needs to shut it down.” Others point the finger higher up the chain. “I think the police commissioner is pretty committed to keeping things in check there, but I know that she probably doesn’t have the backing of the mayor the way she has under other administrations,” said a NYC-based women’s advocate who also declined to be identified. A rep for Mamdani — a passionate supporter of decriminalizing prostitution before being elected mayor — said he “is committed to partnering with local organizations and neighborhood residents to address conditions on Roosevelt Avenue” and is “using every tool available to the city while treating victims and survivors with the care and dignity they deserve.” “Our approach must therefore pair enforcement with the support and opportunity that help people build safer, more stable lives,” said City Hall spokesman Sam Raskin. Many of the johns busted along Roosevelt Avenue this year include ex-cons with long rap sheets. They include John Maddox, 52, who was arrested July 29 on Roosevelt Avenue near 98th Street for allegedly offering an undercover cop $20 for sex; and Mario Sanchez, 31, who was busted while allegedly offering $100 to an undercover cop for sex on June 11 near 80th Street, police sources said. Both were charged with patronizing prostitution, which carries a penalty of up to a year in prison, and pleaded not guilty.  Maddox had 12 prior arrests, including one in 2024 for criminal sale of drugs, and Sanchez was previously arrested five times, police sources said. John, the Manhattan horndog, said residents shouldn’t blame cops for the strip being so seedy. “The police are always around, but it seems like there’s nothing they can do,” John said. “The women know New York laws are lax. Many come from other states . . . That’s what they tell me.”

Results are provided by Google site search. Press Escape to close. Every designer who has ever sketched with a fat marker or a clumsy ballpoint knows the same small frustration. The barrel gets in the way of the exact point you’re trying to control, and by the time you glance past your own knuckles, the line has already wandered somewhere you didn’t plan. That is the specific annoyance Milan-based industrial designer Alberto Essesi set out to fix with the Exclamation Pen, a slim aluminum instrument built around one idea: let the person holding it see straight down to the tip, every single time. Most pens are not designed for sketching. They are designed for writing, which is a different task with different demands. A note-taker doesn’t need to watch the nib travel across the page with surgical precision. A designer roughing out a form, a joint, or a curve does. Essesi, who has spent his career working across design and technology companies before starting his own studio, apparently got tired of choosing between tools that felt good in the hand and tools that actually showed him where the line would land. So he machined his own answer. Designer: Alberto Essesi  The pen itself is carved from solid aluminum blocks and finished in a matte satin coat, and it comes apart into three simple pieces, including a stand that doubles as a cap. The tip is severely tapered, almost aggressively so, which is the whole point. That taper is what clears the sightline and lets the tip stay visible no matter the angle of the hand. When the pen and its stand are placed together, the silhouette reads like a punctuation mark, which is where the name comes from. It’s a small joke buried in a very serious object, and it works because the pen never oversells the gag. The humor sits quietly in the shape, not in the marketing copy.       What strikes me most about this project is how confidently it ignores trends. Pen design right now is dominated by refillable systems, smart pens, and gadgets that track your handwriting for an app you’ll open twice. Essesi went the opposite direction and stripped a writing tool down to geometry and material, betting that the right taper and the right balance point matter more than any added feature. I happen to think that bet pays off. There is something satisfying about a tool that solves a real, physical problem instead of inventing a digital one to sell you a subscription for.  The pen also isn’t new to Essesi’s practice. Around a year before the Exclamation Pen appeared, he shared an earlier, rougher concept online, inspired by a documentary about how early humans used rocks to mark walls. That instinct, wanting a tool stripped back to its most basic gesture, clearly followed him into this refined version. It’s rare to watch a designer’s idea mature in public like that, from a raw sketching stick to a numbered, limited-run object sold through Normal Objects for $168.       And limited is not an exaggeration. Essesi self-produces every batch, and the first three runs reportedly sold out before he could restock. He’s now considering a mirror-polished version alongside the current satin finish, which tells me demand caught even him off guard. There’s a version of this story where that scarcity feels like a marketing trick, but knowing this is a one-person operation machining aluminum by hand, it reads more like a production bottleneck than a strategy.  None of this makes the Exclamation Pen a mass-market object, and it probably shouldn’t be. It’s priced and positioned for people who already care about how a tool feels between their fingers, the same audience that lines up for a well-made notebook or a Japanese mechanical pencil. But the underlying idea, that visibility at the tip is worth designing an entire object around, is one that any pen maker could learn from. Sometimes the most useful design decision isn’t adding something new. It’s removing whatever was blocking the view in the first place. Petrol nozzle Kindly share this story: The Dangote Petroleum Refinery ended August with 630.9 million litres of refined petroleum products in stock as Nigeria continued to import petrol and other fuels, latest data from the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority have shown. The NMDPRA’s August 2026 State of the Midstream and Downstream Sector factsheet showed that the refinery’s closing inventory comprised 360.4 million litres of Premium Motor Spirit (petrol), 137.2 million litres of automotive gas oil (diesel) and 133.3 million litres of aviation turbine kerosene (aviation fuel). The latest NMDPRA figures show that the refinery closed August with more than 630 million litres of products in its tanks, including 360.4 million litres of petrol. At the same time, petrol imports continued, although they declined significantly during the month. Average daily PMS imports fell by 26 per cent from 19.7 million litres in July to 14.6 million litres in August, according to the regulator. Domestic PMS receipts, however, rose by 39 per cent from 25.8 million litres per day in July to 35.9 million litres in August.  The increase in domestic supply pushed total PMS receipts into the country up by 11 per cent from 45.5 million litres per day in July to 50.5 million litres in August. Domestic receipts exceeded imports by 21.3 million litres per day during the month. The Dangote refinery accounted for about 71 per cent of the country’s total PMS receipts in August, supplying almost 36 million litres of petrol daily to the domestic market.See more Punch stories on Google.Add Punch on Google The regulator said the refinery produced an average of 41.94 million litres of PMS daily during the month, supplied 35.87 million litres to the domestic market and exported 9.73 million litres daily.         Its average capacity utilisation stood at 105.21 per cent during August, while its PMS closing stock stood at 360.4 million litres. Beyond petrol, the refinery closed August with 137.2 million litres of diesel and 133.3 million litres of aviation fuel, bringing its combined inventory of the three products to 630.9 million litres. Diesel imports also declined sharply during the month, falling by 84 per cent from 7.9 million litres per day in July to 1.3 million litres in August. Meanwhile, PMS consumption declined by 14 per cent from 48.3 million litres per day in July to 41.5 million litres in August. Govt orders captive coal plants to maximise power output on surging demand Let’s begin with power supply. India has ordered 112 captive coal-fired power plants to operate at maximum capacity from October 1 through December 31, citing an expected rise in electricity demand in the coming months. The plants, which mainly serve industrial facilities, have also been directed to sell surplus electricity through power exchanges and report their generation, power sales, available capacity and coal stocks every week. Investors choose UP because of its large consumer market and infrastructure to match it, says CM Yogi Adityanath Next up, Uttar Pradesh is seeking the Centre’s support for a commercial semiconductor fab in the Jewar region, dedicated rail-cargo links and funding for inter-state transmission. Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath said the state is also working to bring logistics costs down from 13–14 per cent of GSDP to the global benchmark of 8–9 per cent, as it seeks to attract more investment. EV 2Ws industry established now, can do without subsidies: Ather Turning to electric vehicles, Ather Energy said the EV industry is now established and can do without subsidies such as PM E-DRIVE. Ather’s Chief Business Officer Ravneet S Phokela said the company is seeing excess demand, with 50–60 per cent of customers waiting 45–50 days due to production constraints. Its new Maharashtra plant, expected to start operations in December, will help increase monthly capacity to around 77,000 units by early next year. CCPA slaps ₹10 lakh fine on Amazon, Flipkart; ₹5 lakh on JioMart over unregistered herbicide sales Finally, in e-commerce, the Central Consumer Protection Authority has imposed penalties of ₹10 lakh each on Amazon and Flipkart, and ₹5 lakh on JioMart, for selling and advertising an unregistered agro-chemical product called ‘Cyclosinone Herbicide’. The regulator has also directed the platforms to discontinue its sale and advertisement, conduct self-audits and submit compliance reports within 15 days. Royal Caribbean is paying $3 billion for half of Sandals Resorts. The stock sold off before the ink was even dry, and analysts can’t agree why.  A $3 Billion Bet On A New Business Line Royal Caribbean Group confirmed a few days ago (September 23, 2026) that it intends to acquire a 50% equity stake in Sandals and Beaches Resorts, the all-inclusive Caribbean brand. The price is roughly $3bn, valuing the full Sandals portfolio at twice that, or a forward EBITDA multiple of roughly 10x. According to reports, Morgan Stanley is providing committed debt financing; the deal is expected to close in early 2027. Royal Caribbean says its Sandals investment should add to earnings the following year. A joint venture board will be run by Royal Caribbean chairman and CEO, Jason Liberty, and Sandals executive chairman Adam Stewart, who called it: a chance to build on what “my father, Gordon ‘Butch’ Stewart, founded… with the belief that a company built in the Caribbean could stand on the world stage.” Liberty framed it as “an important next step in building a vacation platform.” – SEC Filing Existing Sandals reservations, loyalty accounts, and day-to-day operations are not changing. What is changing is who owns half of them, and that a cruise company with three ship brands, Royal Caribbean, Celebrity, and Silversea, now also owns a chunk of a land-based, adults-only, all-inclusive resort chain it has never operated a single property of before. It also just opened a hotel in Chile to support Antarctica operations for Silversea.     The Market Didn’t Wait For The Deal To Be Signed By the time the rumors hit the wire, Royal Caribbean’s stock had already fallen 6.14% on September 22, closing at a 52-week low, after the Financial Times reported the company was closing in on a move into land-based resorts. That was a full day before anyone confirmed a word of it. By the time the actual terms came out on a day later (September 23), the stock’s two-day decline reached roughly 12%, according to Forbes. It may not have been entirely related to the news, however, as Carnival and Norwegian both slipped too, though both were already down sharply for the year on their own issues. Two Analysts, Two Very Different Reads Stifel’s Steven Wieczynski is on the skeptical side, and his logic is simple: “when we have seen a company diversify away from their core competency, it typically hasn’t worked out in the long-term.” That is a fair historical read. The concept is that cruise lines know how to fill ships, and Royal is very good that that. But running a resort chain, with its own labor model, land costs, and hurricane exposure, is a different business with different risks, and Royal Caribbean has never run one. Goldman’s Lizzie Dove takes the other side, pointing to real synergy potential and the fit with Royal Caribbean’s broader push to call itself a vacation company rather than a cruise line. That framing is not just marketing. Royal Caribbean already sells cruise-and-stay packages, already has a private island and beach club business, and a Caribbean resort partner gives it inventory it does not have to build a ship to sell. Iy industry experience suggests that Dove’s take the better fit, but Wieczynski’s caution is not wrong just because the market’s initial 6% drop came before the deal terms existed.     A factor that didn’t make it into analysis I reviewed is the move from resorts into the cruise space (Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection, Four Seasons Yachts, Aman, Waldorf-Astoria, etc.) Many of those lines have struggled to generate the immediate success investors had hoped a cross over could produce. Taking a step back, however, a Royal Caribbean-Sandals JV is at its heart the same market. Both companies focus on all-inclusive products, they both sell sun and sand and service, and their customer list is likely full of many of the same clients. Celebrity might be a closer fit to Sandals, while Beaches and Royal Caribbean are a better fit. Still, the transition into travel products outside of their core does feel possibly problematic. Why Sandals, Why Now Sandals is adults-only, couples-focused, all-inclusive, however it also owns Beaches, a family-friendly all-inclusive brand in many of the same island destinations. Royal Caribbean’s core brand is family cruising. This puts Royal Caribbean’s vacation dollars in front of a customer who might have been unlikely to pursue it. A few years ago, 90% of all Americans had never been on a cruise and while that’s changed especially since COVID, there are only so many floating cities one can put in the water before growth needs to come from somewhere else. The bigger context is that cruise lines have spent the last few years buying or building private islands and beach clubs precisely because the margin on land-based, all-inclusive time is very good, and Royal Caribbean already knows that math from its own destinations. Buying half of an operator that has been running that exact model successfully for decades is a faster way to scale it than building from scratch, even at a 10-times multiple.     One more important consideration is an industry parallel in Disney. Royal has been open that offering three and four-day sailings from Cape Canaveral and South Florida is compete more with Disney World than with other cruise lines. But the House of Mouse is also another guide to how this transition might be successful. Disney has been a constant evolution of the core brand from California to Florida, to resorts around the world. Its Aulani resort in Hawaii is a property across oceans in either direction from its nearest theme park and yet the brand is successful. Disney Cruise Lines is less than 30 years old but commands a premium because it translates the brand so well. It’s fair to look at the Disney brand and determine it to be uniquely exceptional, but loyalty to Royal Caribbean is growing and only getting stronger. Many book Royal because of its private island experiences like Coco Cay and the brand has expanded that model all over the Caribbean but may be in a position to develop that popular experience in a new way. Conclusion Analyst reactions and investor sell-offs were premature. A 6% drop on an unconfirmed report, a day before anyone had seen a term sheet, is a reflex and not a particularly adept one. The bare economics of the deal with a 10-times multiple and debt financing without changing how Sandals operates day-to-day, are sound business fundamentals. Whether Royal’s investment pays off comes down to something no analyst can yet price in: whether Royal Caribbean, a company that has never run a hotel, can be a good half-owner of one without getting in its own way. My personal prediction is that it’s just a matter of time before RCCL buys the other half of the portfolio and Sandals & Beaches are more naturally integrated into the company’s ecosystem. Whether you're a new reader or just missed it the first time around, we’re digging into the Bike EXIF archives to revisit some of our all-time favorite builds. This article was originally published on November 27, 2023. The modern-day Honda CB350 is one of those motorcycles we wished was available in more parts of the world. It first broke cover in India, where it's produced, and later rolled out to Japan as the rebadged GB350. You can get it in Taiwan too, where it's officially called the Honda H'ness CB350—but you can forget about buying one in Europe or the USA. That's a real shame, because the Honda CB350 is about as adorable and approachable as factory bikes get. Its 348.4 cc single-cylinder engine squeezes out 21 hp and 30 Nm, and it sports modern amenities like LED lighting. It's not too bad looking either; handsome enough in stock trim to give bigger modern classics a run for their money. As cute as it is though, there's always room for improvement. Mark Huang of Mark Motorcycles in Taipei, Taiwan shares this sentiment—which is why he's developed a stylish collection of bolt-on parts for the Honda CB350 and GB350. Plug-and-play kits are becoming increasingly popular among pragmatic custom motorcycle builders who are looking for a steady income to keep the lights on. Expensive one-off custom bikes are great to ogle, but building them is time-consuming. A steady supply of custom parts is good for business—and it gives you a stash to dip into if you need to make big changes quickly. There's nothing over-the-top about Mark's scrambler-inspired take on the humble Honda CB350, but that's entirely by design. “Because the CB350 is a perfectly proportioned motorcycle,” he tells us, “I only made changes to a few parts to make the bike better reflect my style. And so that the bike can be changed quickly, the parts can be replaced without modifying the frame.” Still, Mark's casual approach belies how much work went into getting this kit from concept to production. He started by buying a suitable donor to use as a test bed, then stripped off everything that he figured could be improved. The OEM fuel tank and side covers were deemed tidy enough to stay, but the Honda's modern-looking fenders were binned. Mark designed new fiber-reinforced polymer fenders with a classic street scrambler aesthetic. The fenders ship with all the brackets needed to fit them, and the rear fender wears a stylish Lucas-style taillight. Mark's Honda CB350 also swapped its alloy hoops for an all-new set of spoked wheels with alloy rims. They measure 19” up front and 18” out back, and wear Shinko dual-sport tires. A 5.5” Bates-style headlight replaces the stock unit, with a neat Koso speedo perched just above it. The cockpit also features high, laid-back handlebars fitted with vintage-style switches, new grips, and a single underslung mirror. Mark wisely kept the bike's original handlebar clamp; a branded part that recalls the designs on classic Hondas. It's worth mentioning that all of these parts don't just come with the bracketry needed to mount them, but also every last wire and connector you need to make it all work. Mark's gone to great lengths to make sure that there's zero guesswork when putting everything together. It's the same story with the exhaust, where a slim reverse cone muffler attaches to the stock header via a custom-made connector pipe. Other add-ons include new rear shocks and classically styled turn signals mounted on bolt-on brackets. Perched atop the CB350 is an impossibly chic seat that looks more custom than off-the-shelf. You can order it in either leather or a synthetic fabric. Finishing the build off is an eye-popping 70s-inspired paint job, courtesy of Mark's friend, Jeffery. All of the parts shown here are already available, and Mark has wasted no time in putting them to use. No sooner had he buttoned up his prototype build, than he got a commission for a near-identical Honda CB350 [below right]. The client wanted a black and grey livery and lower handlebars, but the rest of the spec sheet is the same. And with its more subdued tank graphics, it could easily be mistaken for a neatly restored classic. We would have been perfectly happy with a bone-stock Honda CB350 in the garage—until we saw these two bikes. The combination of the CB's best bits (like its beautiful black and chrome engine), and Mark's judicious changes, has taken it from unassuming entry-level retro to irresistible street scrambler. The Houthi-run health ministry accused the Saudi Air Force of committing an "abominable crime," vowing to retaliate. The Houthis' account of the attack cannot be independently verified.  Yemen's Houthi rebels on Sunday accused the Saudi Arabian Air Force of having struck a shopping area around the central market of Taiz. The Iran-aligned Houthis said at least seven people had been killed and dozens injured. The group's Al-Masirah TV channel showed footage of large plumes of smoke and a destroyed warehouse stacked with food in cardboard boxes. Al-Masirah TV also reported that children were among those wounded, citing the Houthis' health ministry. Taiz is currently under the control of Yemeni government forces, but it has long been besieged by Houthi fighters and remains one of the main fronts in the country's civil war. Taiz is located in southwestern Yemen.  The escalation in fighting comes after a fragile truce between Yemeni government forces and Houthi rebels broke down months ago and new regional tensions sparked by the Iran war. The Houthi health ministry accused the Saudi Air Force of committing an "abominable crime," saying it was directly and deliberately targeting civilian sites in Taiz. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree accused Saudi Arabia of launching two air raids that hit the market, adding that blood was "unjustly and aggressively spilled" in a statement posted online. The group has vowed to retaliate.  The claims made by the Houthis cannot be independently verified.   In response to the Houthi report, troops loyal to the internationally recognized government in Yemen confirmed that their air force had struck a Houthi depot and vehicles in the area. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The civil war in Yemen began in 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa from the Saudi-backed government. They went on to take control of vast swaths of the country's north. Saudi Arabia joined forces against the Houthis the following year, leading an international coalition against them. But so far, Yemen's government forces have not been able to effectively repel the latest Houthi offensive. Fighting has spiked in September as the Houthis launched a lightning offensive that saw them seize Yemen's entire Red Sea coast. The rebels have also launched a blockade on Saudi energy exports to coincide with Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Renewed clashes are is under way in several parts of the country, with at least 125,000 people displaced by it. The Yemeni government has meanwhile called for a general mobilization, urging Yemenis to join the army and security forces.  Yemen is one of the poorest in the world and remains gripped by a vast humanitarian crisis. Israel escalates retaliatory measures as Western sanctions target illegal West Bank settlements. Save Share Israel has revoked the diplomatic status of Dutch diplomats at the Netherlands’ ‌Representative Office in Ramallah, Israel’s Foreign Ministry has said. The countermeasure announced on Sunday comes in response to the Dutch government’s ban on ⁠imports originating ⁠from Israeli settlements in the ⁠occupied West Bank. In a statement posted on X, Israel’s Foreign Minister Gidoen Saar said, “If the Netherlands wishes to continue representing its interests with the Palestinians, it may do so from Palestinian Authority territory, rather than from the territory of the State of Israel.” Israel informed the Dutch embassy that “diplomats operating in Ramallah must return their Israeli-issued diplomatic documentation within seven days”. Saar said, “Last month, we removed the Dutch delegation from the International Support Center for Gaza in Kiryat Gat, following actions taken by the Dutch Government against Israel. I reiterate: Israel will not ignore measures intended to harm it. Any country that acts in a hostile and unilateral manner against Israel will lose influence and relevance in the region.” Carne Ross, a former senior British diplomat and founder of the non-profit advisory group Independent Diplomat, told Al Jazeera that “the fact that Israel is chucking out Dutch diplomats who are essentially diplomats to Palestine, to the Palestinian population in the West Bank, I don’t think is that significant, except to indicate Israel’s growing diplomatic isolation.”      Israel has enacted a series of retaliatory measures in response to the United Kingdom, France and Canada announcing sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements. Earlier this month, Israel announced a seven-day deadline for the removal of British representatives from the International Gaza Support Center as one of four countermeasures against the UK for imposing sanctions on illegal settlements in the West Bank. The Netherlands brought its ban into force on September 22. The Dutch measure goes further than some others. It bans the import, purchase and sale of goods from illegal Israeli settlements, as well as services facilitating that trade. Bilateral trade between the Netherlands and Israel totalled about $4.8bn last year. Its significance extends beyond the Dutch market, with the Netherlands serving as a major gateway for goods entering the rest of Europe. The legal non-profit Global Echo group said the Netherlands accounted for a third of agricultural exports from Israel’s illegal settlements and nearly half of those destined for the European Union.
